title: Apple blames 'internal update' as iCloud, App Store and Apple Pay go down for thousands
summary: Thousands of Apple users were locked out of iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay on Tuesday after an internal update knocked out several of the company's online services; Apple said the failure was not a cyberattack and most systems were back within hours.
content: Thousands of Apple users were locked out of iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay on Tuesday after an internal software update knocked out several of the company's online services, in the latest of a run of technology failures to hit American users this week. Reports of problems began to surge shortly before noon Eastern Time, according to the outage tracker Downdetector, with users complaining that they had been signed out of their Apple accounts without warning, could not sign back in, and could not download apps or pay with their phones. Apple confirmed outages affecting the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device, and said iCloud account sign-in "may be slow or unavailable" for all users. By Tuesday afternoon the company said most systems were back up, and its status page later listed the affected services as operating normally. "Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," Apple said in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." The company told Bloomberg that the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack, a point that mattered because the outage arrived on a day when online security was already in the headlines. For many users the first sign of trouble was an unexpected message on their own device. People reported being signed out of iCloud and then asked, repeatedly, to verify their identity before they could get back in. Others found the App Store would not load, or that downloads stalled halfway. Some said they could not set up a new iPhone at all, because activation runs through Apple's servers. Apple Pay users reported failed or stalled payments at the point of sale, according to Downdetector. The scale of the disruption is hard to pin down from complaint trackers alone, because Downdetector counts only the people who take the trouble to report a problem. Even so, the pattern was unmistakable. According to Downdetector, reports of Apple Pay problems began rising at about 11:40 a.m. Eastern Time and peaked at about 12:15 p.m., while reports about iCloud began surging just before noon and reports across Apple's services jumped into the thousands by about 12:29 p.m., according to Engadget. The numbers then fell sharply during the early afternoon as services came back. The problems were not confined to the United States. Users in the United Arab Emirates reported Apple Pay and iCloud failures on Tuesday evening local time, according to Gulf News, and Times Now reported complaints from Brazil, Greece and Latvia as well. That reach is a reminder of how far Apple's account system extends: a single sign-in underpins a phone, a watch, a laptop, a payment card and a family's photo library at the same time, so a failure in the sign-in system can feel like losing the device itself. What made Tuesday stand out was not the outage alone but its timing. It came a day after a software bug at the technology provider behind JPMorgan Chase disrupted online banking for millions of Americans, an incident Global Wire covered on Monday, when [a software fault at the bank's technology supplier rippled through Chase, Bank of America and the Zelle payment network](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/ar/articles/us-banks-outage-chase-software-bug-november-2026). The same week also brought a widespread Microsoft Outlook failure and a United Airlines systems outage that disrupted flights. There is no evidence that the incidents are connected, and they appear to have different causes: the bank outage was traced to a software bug, while Apple blamed its own internal update. But the pile-up has fed public anxiety about how much daily life now depends on a handful of large platforms working without interruption. That anxiety is understandable, but the details matter. The bank outage and the Apple outage were both traced by the companies involved to their own software, not to an outside attacker. Apple's statement ruling out a cyberattack came after the company was pressed on the question, and US officials investigating the bank disruption likewise said they had found no evidence of one. The distinction matters to users deciding whether to change a password or check a bank statement: an internal failure is an inconvenience, while a breach would be a reason to act. Still, the episode leaves Apple with questions to answer. Its public status page was slow to reflect what users were plainly experiencing, at one point showing many services as available while thousands of people reported failures. That gap between the official status and the lived experience is a familiar frustration with large technology companies, and it is one reason outage trackers such as Downdetector have become a first stop for users trying to work out whether the problem is their phone or the service itself. Apple has not said what the internal update changed, which systems it touched, or what it will do to stop a repeat. For users, the practical advice is simple and does not require any action. Anyone signed out of iCloud during the outage should be able to sign back in now that services are restored, and Apple said no user data was affected. Anyone who changed a password or payment detail in a panic during the disruption may want to check that their devices have the current details. And anyone setting up a new device should find activation working again. The outage lasted hours rather than days, and by the end of the working day in the United States most of Apple's services were operating normally, according to [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/2026/11/17/apple-services-outage/92827849007/). But for a company whose pitch is that its products simply work, a morning in which millions of people could not sign in, download an app or pay for a coffee with their phone is a reminder that even the most polished systems can be brought down by a routine update.
